note: HAND-WRITTEN plain-language descriptions, for a reader who has never encountered a substance and does not know what it is. PsychonautWiki cannot supply these: its `summary` field is a scraped warning box that is frequently junk ("Summary sheet: MDMA MDMA"), and its `effects` field returns only the substance's own name. Both were checked against the live API on 2026-08-10 before writing these by hand. A second batch was written on 2026-08-15 for substances whose ordinary identity IS the description - a supplement, a spice, an over-the-counter box, a prescription somebody already holds. Those did not need a published effects write-up to be describable, and leaving them blank was the wrong call: a reader who does not know that myristicin is nutmeg cannot assess anything else on the page. Where the effects genuinely are not documented, the description says so rather than inventing them.
rules: Say what it IS and what people take it FOR. Someone who does not know cannot assess a warning about it.
No dosing, no route advice, no how-to. Dose ranges already live in their own section with their own caveats.
Neither advertise nor frighten. 'Euphoric' oversells; 'deadly poison' is the fear-based framing EVIDENCE.md rejects. Describe.
Name the ordinary medical use where there is one - most people meet oxycodone, ketamine and diazepam in a hospital first.
Plain words. Roughly an 8th-grade reading level, no pharmacology unless it changes what someone would do.
Where the thing has an ordinary identity - a supplement, a spice, an OTC box, a prescription - lead with that. What it says on the packaging is a checkable fact and it is what the reader recognizes.
Where nobody has published what it DOES, say so plainly and still say what it IS. An absence of effects data is not an absence of identity.

descriptions.alcohol: The drug in beer, wine and spirits. Chemically it is ethanol. It is a depressant, so it slows the brain and body. That is what makes people relaxed, talkative and unsteady. Coordination, judgement and memory get worse as the dose goes up. The liver clears it at a roughly fixed rate per hour.
descriptions.cannabis: The dried flower of the cannabis plant, smoked, vaped or eaten. Effects vary a lot between people and between strains. Usually it brings relaxation, changed senses and hunger. Some people get anxiety or a racing heart instead. Eaten, it comes on slowly and lasts far longer.
descriptions.mdma: A stimulant that also does something to your feelings, sold as ecstasy or molly, in pills or powder. People take it for warmth, closeness and energy, mostly around other people and music. It pushes up your body temperature and heart rate. A lot of what gets sold under these names is not MDMA at all.
descriptions.lsd: A psychedelic, usually sold on small squares of blotter paper. It changes how you see, think and feel for eight to twelve hours, which is longer than most people expect the first time. Chemically it is a semi-synthetic ergoline, active in the microgram range: a dose is a few tens of millionths of a gram.
descriptions.psilocybin-mushrooms: Mushrooms containing psilocybin, sometimes called magic mushrooms or shrooms, usually eaten dried or brewed into tea. They bring visual changes, shifts in thinking and mood, and often strong emotion, for about four to six hours. The body converts psilocybin into psilocin, which is the compound that does the work.
descriptions.ketamine: An anesthetic used in hospitals and by vets, also used as a powder recreationally. It makes you feel detached from your body and your surroundings. At higher amounts, movement and response stop altogether. That is called a k-hole. It is a dissociative, acting mainly by blocking NMDA receptors.
descriptions.cocaine: A stimulant made from the coca plant, sold as a white powder. It makes you alert, confident and full of energy, often for under an hour. That short run is why people keep going back for more. It strains the heart. Mixed with alcohol, the body makes a third substance that is harder on the heart than either alone.
descriptions.crack-cocaine: Cocaine cooked into a smokable rock. Same drug as powder cocaine. Smoking gets it there faster and it wears off sooner. So people redose more often, and dependence builds more easily.
descriptions.heroin: An opioid made from morphine, sold as a white or brown powder or as black tar. It relieves pain, brings on heavy sedation, and slows breathing. Across much of the US, what is sold as heroin now has fentanyl in it, or is fentanyl. Strength can change from one batch to the next.
descriptions.fentanyl: A synthetic opioid used in hospitals for severe pain, and now the main opioid in the US street supply. It relieves pain and slows breathing like other opioids. It works in far smaller amounts than heroin, so it is very hard to mix evenly. Two scoops from the same bag can be different strengths.
descriptions.methamphetamine: A strong stimulant, sold as a crystal or a powder. It brings energy, focus and confidence, and it lasts far longer than cocaine. Heavy or long-term use is linked to lost sleep and weight, tooth damage, and paranoia or psychosis that can last after you stop.
descriptions.amphetamine: A stimulant, prescribed as Adderall for ADHD and also used without a prescription. It sharpens focus, gives you energy, keeps you awake and kills appetite. The prescribed and street versions are the same drug — the difference is that a prescription comes with a known strength.
descriptions.methylphenidate: A stimulant prescribed as Ritalin or Concerta, mostly for ADHD. It sharpens focus and gives you energy, and does not last as long as amphetamine.
descriptions.alprazolam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Xanax for anxiety and panic. It calms and sedates, and it interferes with laying down memories of the hours it is active. Pressed pills sold as Xanax frequently contain a different benzodiazepine, or none at all.
descriptions.diazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Valium for anxiety, muscle spasm and alcohol withdrawal. It sedates, relaxes muscle and lowers anxiety. It lasts longer than most of its family: what the body breaks it down into keeps working for a day or more.
descriptions.oxycodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as OxyContin or Percocet. It kills pain, sedates you and brings euphoria. Pills sold as oxycodone outside a pharmacy — especially ones stamped M30 — are very often pressed fentanyl instead.
descriptions.codeine: A weaker opioid, in some prescription cough syrups and pain tablets. Your body turns it into morphine. How much it turns varies a lot from person to person, so the same tablet hits two people differently.
descriptions.buprenorphine: An opioid used to treat opioid dependence and pain, prescribed as Suboxone or Subutex. It sits on the same receptors without doing the same thing, which takes away withdrawal and cravings. Because it grips those receptors so tightly, taking it too soon after another opioid can throw you straight into withdrawal.
descriptions.tramadol: A prescription painkiller. It works partly as a weak opioid and partly on serotonin and norepinephrine, the way some antidepressants do. That second part is why it reacts badly with antidepressants and raises the chance of a seizure.
descriptions.kratom: The leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, taken as powder, capsules or tea. Smaller amounts feel more like a stimulant, larger amounts more like a mild opioid. Some people use it for pain, or to get through opioid withdrawal. Using it regularly can build dependence, with a withdrawal of its own.
descriptions.ghb: A depressant sold as a salty liquid, used recreationally and sometimes for sleep. It sedates and disinhibits, and the amount that produces those effects and the amount that produces unconsciousness are very close together. It occurs naturally in the body in tiny amounts, and GBL converts into it after swallowing.
descriptions.dmt: A very short, very intense psychedelic, usually smoked or vaped. It arrives within seconds and is usually over in fifteen to thirty minutes. It is also what makes ayahuasca work. With an MAOI it lasts hours instead. That combination reacts badly with a lot of medications.
descriptions.mescaline: A psychedelic found in peyote, San Pedro and related cacti, used in Indigenous ceremony for a very long time. Visual and emotional changes lasting roughly ten to twelve hours. Peyote grows slowly and is under threat, and its ceremonial use is legally protected for members of the Native American Church.
descriptions.2c-b: A synthetic psychedelic with a stimulant edge, sold as pills or powder. Shorter than LSD — usually four to eight hours. It belongs to a family of near-identical chemicals with very different strengths. Mixing one up for another is the usual way people get hurt with it.
descriptions.nitrous: Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, used by dentists and to charge whipped cream canisters. Breathed in, you get about a minute of dizziness and distortion. Two specific dangers. Breathing it without oxygen can suffocate you. Using a lot of it strips out your vitamin B12, which causes nerve damage.
descriptions.pregabalin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain, seizures and anxiety, sold as Lyrica. It is a depressant: calming, sedating, and at higher doses euphoric. It works on calcium channels in nerve cells rather than on the benzodiazepine or opioid systems.
descriptions.gabapentin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain and seizures, sold as Neurontin. Like pregabalin it sedates you and stacks with opioids and alcohol. People tend to assume it is harmless because it is everywhere and handed out freely.
descriptions.methadone: An opioid used both to treat opioid dependence and for pain. It relieves pain and withdrawal without the sharp peak of heroin or fentanyl. It also lasts far longer than either, often more than a day. Because it clears slowly, it accumulates over the first few days of regular dosing before levelling off.
descriptions.morphine: The original opioid painkiller, made from the opium poppy and still used in hospitals for severe pain. Nearly every other opioid gets measured against it.
descriptions.hydrocodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as Vicodin or Norco, usually mixed with acetaminophen. That mix matters: taking extra tablets to get more opioid also means more acetaminophen, and acetaminophen wrecks your liver.
descriptions.hydromorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Dilaudid, used in hospitals for severe pain. A good deal stronger than morphine, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.oxymorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Opana. Stronger than oxycodone, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.tapentadol: A prescription painkiller that acts both as an opioid and on norepinephrine, in a single molecule. The opioid action relieves pain; the second action is the same mechanism some antidepressants use.
descriptions.pethidine: An older opioid painkiller, also called meperidine or Demerol, once common in childbirth and surgery. Used far less now, because something it breaks down into builds up with repeated doses and can cause seizures.
descriptions.dihydrocodeine: An opioid painkiller about as strong as codeine, found in some prescription tablets and cough medicines.
descriptions.o-desmethyltramadol: What the body turns tramadol into, and the part that actually relieves pain. It is sometimes sold on its own, including in products marketed as herbal, at strengths that are not stated.
descriptions.dextropropoxyphene: An opioid painkiller, pulled from the US and much of Europe. It caused heart rhythm problems at amounts not far above a normal dose.
descriptions.acetylfentanyl: A fentanyl analogue — a chemical cousin of fentanyl. It was never made as a medicine and turns up in the street opioid supply. Like fentanyl, it works in tiny amounts, so it is hard to mix evenly.
descriptions.sufentanil: A hospital opioid, used in surgery and epidurals. It relieves pain and sedates like other opioids. By weight it is far stronger than fentanyl, working in the low microgram range.
descriptions.u-47700: A synthetic opioid, sometimes sold as pink or U4. It was made for research and never approved as a medicine. It shows up as a powder, or pressed into fake pills.
descriptions.dextromethorphan: The cough suppressant in many over-the-counter cold medicines, often labeled DXM. At ordinary doses it suppresses coughing; at much larger ones it acts as a dissociative, producing detachment and altered perception. Cold medicines often combine it with acetaminophen or antihistamines, which are different drugs with their own effects.
descriptions.pcp: A dissociative anesthetic, also called angel dust, dropped from medical use because of how confused and agitated people were as it wore off. It leaves you detached from your body and your surroundings, and does unpredictable things to mood and behavior.
descriptions.mephedrone: A stimulant, also called 4-MMC or meow meow, sold as powder or in capsules. Energy and sociability for a short time, which is exactly why people redose.
descriptions.3-mmc: A stimulant closely related to mephedrone, sold after mephedrone got banned in a lot of countries. Similar effects, similarly short.
descriptions.a-pvp: A stimulant that lasts a long time, sometimes called flakka, part of the cathinone family. Effects can run for many hours, and at higher amounts it brings agitation, sleeplessness and confusion.
descriptions.methylone: A stimulant with a mild emotional edge, chemically related to MDMA but much weaker on that front. It has been sold as MDMA, and mixed into things labeled MDMA.
descriptions.mda: A psychedelic stimulant closely related to MDMA, sometimes called sally. Lasts longer than MDMA, with more visual effect and less of the emotional warmth.
descriptions.mdea: A drug closely related to MDMA, sometimes called eve, with a milder emotional effect.
descriptions.gbl: An industrial solvent that the body turns into GHB after you swallow it. The effects are the same as GHB's. So is the small gap between the amount that gets you high and the amount that puts you out.
descriptions.baclofen: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasticity, sometimes used for alcohol dependence. It is a depressant and adds to what opioids and alcohol are already doing. Stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal.
descriptions.mdai: A drug related to MDMA that brings emotional warmth without much stimulation. Sometimes sold as a legal stand-in for MDMA.
descriptions.5-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sold as an MDMA substitute, and often lasting a lot longer than people expect.
descriptions.6-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sometimes called benzo fury, sold as an MDMA substitute. It comes on slowly, which is how people end up taking more than they meant to. Then it lasts a long time.
descriptions.caffeine: The stimulant in coffee, tea and energy drinks, and a very common cutting agent in powders sold as something else. On its own it is mild; mixed into a stimulant it makes a bag look bigger without making it stronger.
descriptions.nicotine: The drug in tobacco and vapes. It is a stimulant: it sharpens attention briefly, raises heart rate, and builds dependence faster than almost anything else here. It acts on the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which is where the name comes from.
descriptions.clonazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Klonopin for seizures and panic. Long-acting. Like the rest of its family it stacks with opioids and alcohol, and stopping suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.lorazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Ativan for anxiety and seizures. Shorter-acting than diazepam. Same two rules as the rest of the family. It stacks with opioids and alcohol. Coming off it has to be gradual.
descriptions.zolpidem: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Ambien. It brings on sleep quickly and wears off fast. It is not a benzodiazepine, but it works on the same GABA-A system. It is known for people doing things while apparently awake and not remembering afterwards.
descriptions.zopiclone: A sleeping pill, sold as Imovane or Zimovane. Like zolpidem it is not a benzodiazepine but acts on the same GABA-A system. It commonly leaves a metallic taste in the mouth.
descriptions.eszopiclone: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Lunesta. Closely related to zopiclone and carries the same warning about mixing with opioids or alcohol.
descriptions.etizolam: A benzodiazepine-type drug — a thienodiazepine — prescribed in a few countries and sold widely online everywhere else. It sedates and reduces anxiety like the rest of the family. It is often what is actually in a pill sold as Xanax, and strength varies enormously batch to batch.
descriptions.flualprazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never a medicine anywhere. It turns up pressed into fake Xanax, and it is much stronger than alprazolam. So a pill that looks familiar can be far more sedating than expected.
descriptions.flubromazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never approved as a medicine. Very strong in very small amounts and long-lasting, which is a bad combination when nobody knows how much is in a pill.
descriptions.metizolam: A designer benzodiazepine sold online, never a medicine. Like the others in this group, the real problem is that the amount in any given pill is unknown.
descriptions.deschloroetizolam: A designer benzodiazepine related to etizolam, never approved as a medicine and not made to any consistent strength.
descriptions.phenibut: A Russian anxiety medicine sold as a supplement in the US. It is a depressant and adds to alcohol and opioids. Dependence builds faster than people expect, and the withdrawal is genuinely severe — closer to benzodiazepine withdrawal than to a hangover.
descriptions.f-phenibut: A stronger, faster version of phenibut, sold as a supplement. Same dependence and same severe withdrawal, reached sooner.
descriptions.modafinil: A prescription wakefulness drug, sold as Provigil, used for narcolepsy and shift work. It keeps you awake without much of a stimulant rush. It speeds up how the liver clears some medicines, which matters most for hormonal birth control.
descriptions.armodafinil: A longer-lasting version of modafinil, prescribed as Nuvigil, with the same effects and the same interaction with hormonal birth control.
descriptions.psilocin: What your body turns psilocybin into, and the part that actually does something. It is also what is measured when mushrooms are tested.
descriptions.datura: A plant — jimsonweed or thornapple — containing deliriants. This is not a psychedelic: people experience convincing hallucinations they cannot tell from real, often with no memory afterwards. The amount varies wildly between plants, and even between parts of the same plant. The gap between an active dose and a poisonous one is small.
descriptions.ayahuasca: A brew from South America combining a DMT-containing plant with an MAOI plant, traditionally used in ceremony. The MAOI is what makes it last hours rather than minutes. It is also the part that reacts badly with many antidepressants and with some foods.
descriptions.changa: DMT absorbed onto an herb blend that includes an MAOI, made to be smoked. It lasts longer than smoked DMT alone, and the MAOI brings the same medication interactions ayahuasca has.
descriptions.melatonin: A hormone the brain makes at night to time sleep. The version sold in shops is a supplement, taken to fall asleep or to reset after a time-zone change. It is not a sedative and does not knock you out: it shifts when you feel sleepy rather than forcing it.
descriptions.myristicin: A compound in nutmeg, and the reason large amounts of the spice affect people. Swallowing a lot of it is well documented as unpleasant: hours of nausea, a racing heart, dry mouth and confusion. It comes on slowly and can last a day or more.
descriptions.diphenhydramine: The antihistamine in Benadryl and many night-time cold medicines. It causes drowsiness at normal doses. At high doses it is a deliriant: confusion and hallucinations that people find frightening. It also adds to the sedation of anything else that slows you down.
descriptions.cannabidiol: CBD — a compound from the cannabis plant sold in oils, drinks and gummies. It does not get you high the way THC does. It is sold for anxiety, pain and sleep. The evidence for that is thin. The exception is two rare seizure disorders, where a prescription version works well. Products vary wildly in what they actually contain.
descriptions.kava: A drink made from the root of a Pacific Islands plant. It is traditional in Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa. In the US it is sold in kava bars and as capsules. It relaxes the body and calms without clouding thinking much.
descriptions.blue-lotus: A water lily used in ancient Egyptian art and ritual, sold now as a tea, a vape or a tincture. People report mild calm and drowsiness. Almost none of it has been studied properly, so what it does at the amounts people take is not established.
descriptions.creatine: A sports supplement, one of the most studied there is. It helps muscles produce short bursts of power, so people take it for strength training. It is not psychoactive — it is here because it turns up in stacks alongside things that are.
descriptions.theanine: An amino acid found in tea leaves, sold as a supplement and often paired with caffeine. People take it to take the edge off caffeine's jitteriness. Effects are mild; it is here because it is a common ingredient in energy and "focus" products.
descriptions.theacrine: A compound related to caffeine, found in kucha tea and sold in energy and pre-workout products. It is stimulating and appears to build less tolerance than caffeine. Human research on it is limited.
descriptions.alpha-gpc: A choline supplement sold for memory and focus, and used in some countries as a prescription drug after a stroke. It is a building block your body uses to make a brain chemical involved in attention. Sold over the counter in the US as a nootropic.
descriptions.choline-bitartrate: A cheap, common form of choline, an essential nutrient found in eggs and liver. Sold as a supplement for memory and often taken alongside nootropics. Little of it reaches the brain compared with the other forms sold for the same purpose.
descriptions.citicoline: A choline supplement sold for memory and attention. In parts of Europe and Asia it is a prescription medicine, given after strokes and head injuries. Sold over the counter in the US.
descriptions.n-acetylcysteine: NAC — a supplement, and also a hospital medicine, where it is the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning. It is a precursor to glutathione, one of the body's own antioxidants. Over the counter it is sold for the lungs, the liver, and on thinner evidence for cravings.
descriptions.sam-e: A supplement sold for mood and joints, and a prescription antidepressant in several European countries. It is a substance the body already makes, used in reactions all over the body. It acts on the same serotonin system antidepressants do.
descriptions.tyrosine: An amino acid from ordinary protein in food, sold as a supplement. Your body uses it to build dopamine and adrenaline, which is why it is marketed for focus and for performing under stress. Effects in well-rested people are small.
descriptions.5-hydroxytryptophan: 5-HTP — a supplement the body converts directly into serotonin, sold for mood and sleep. It is the intermediate step between tryptophan and serotonin, which is why it raises serotonin levels rather than acting on a receptor itself.
descriptions.galantamine: A prescription medicine for Alzheimer's disease, derived from snowdrops, and sold as a supplement for lucid dreaming. It raises levels of a brain chemical involved in memory.
descriptions.naloxone: The overdose-reversal drug, sold as Narcan and as a generic nasal spray or injection. It knocks opioids off their receptors and restores breathing, usually within a few minutes. It has no effect on a person with no opioids in them. It wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, sooner than most opioids do.
descriptions.clonidine: A blood-pressure medicine also prescribed for ADHD, anxiety, hot flushes and — commonly — to take the edge off opioid withdrawal. It lowers blood pressure and heart rate, so it can cause fainting, and it stacks with anything else that sedates.
descriptions.promethazine: A prescription antihistamine used for nausea, allergies and as a sedative, and the other half of "lean" when mixed with codeine cough syrup. It is heavily sedating on its own and adds to the breathing suppression of opioids.
descriptions.prochlorperazine: A prescription medicine for severe nausea, vomiting and vertigo. It is sedating, and it can cause distressing muscle stiffness and restlessness in a minority of people who take it.
descriptions.quetiapine: An antipsychotic sold as Seroquel, prescribed for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and very widely prescribed off-label at low doses as a sleeping aid. Strongly sedating.
descriptions.mirtazapine: An antidepressant also prescribed for sleep and appetite. It is sedating, most noticeably at lower doses, and it increases appetite. It acts on serotonin and norepinephrine receptors rather than by blocking reuptake the way SSRIs do.
descriptions.risperidone: An antipsychotic prescribed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and irritability in autism. Sometimes given in emergency rooms to somebody in a drug-induced psychosis.
descriptions.haloperidol: An older antipsychotic, best known as the drug given by injection in emergency rooms to calm somebody agitated or psychotic. It can cause severe muscle stiffness and restlessness.
descriptions.ephedrine: A stimulant from the ephedra plant. In the US it is sold over the counter for congestion and asthma. It raises heart rate and blood pressure. Sales are tracked, because it can be used to make methamphetamine.
descriptions.benzydamine: An anti-inflammatory sold over the counter in many countries as a throat spray, gargle or lozenge for mouth and throat pain. Swallowed in large amounts it causes hallucinations and agitation, which is the only reason it appears here.
descriptions.carisoprodol: A muscle relaxant, prescribed as Soma. It sedates and relaxes muscle. The body turns part of it into meprobamate, an old sedative. That is why it is habit-forming, and why it stacks with opioids and alcohol.
descriptions.tizanidine: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasms and spasticity. It lowers blood pressure and is sedating.
descriptions.progesterone: A hormone your body makes, also prescribed as a medicine in hormone therapy, contraception and fertility treatment. It is on this list because it changes how the body handles some other drugs, not because it is taken to get high.
descriptions.lisdexamfetamine: Vyvanse — a prescription stimulant for ADHD and binge-eating disorder. It does nothing until your body turns it into dexamfetamine. That is why it comes on slowly, and why it is harder to misuse than other amphetamine pills.
descriptions.dextroamphetamine: A prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy, and the more active half of Adderall. It increases alertness, focus and heart rate.
descriptions.memantine: A prescription medicine for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. It acts on the same receptor as ketamine but far more weakly and much more slowly, and it is not sedating.
descriptions.piracetam: The original "nootropic" — the word was coined for it. Sold as a supplement in the US and prescribed in parts of Europe for cognitive decline and involuntary muscle jerks. Evidence in healthy people is weak.
descriptions.aniracetam: A nootropic in the same family as piracetam, sold as a supplement in the US and as a prescription medicine in some countries. Marketed for memory and anxiety; human evidence is limited.
descriptions.oxiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family, sold as a supplement and marketed for memory and focus. Studied mostly in cognitive decline rather than in healthy people.
descriptions.pramiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family, sold as a supplement. Marketed for memory; the small amount of research on it is in brain injury, not in healthy people.
descriptions.phenylpiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family developed in the Soviet space program, sold as a supplement. Unlike the others it is noticeably stimulating, and it is banned in competitive sport for that reason.
descriptions.adrafinil: A supplement your liver converts into modafinil, the prescription wakefulness drug. It is sold over the counter in the US because it is not itself a controlled substance. The conversion is hard on the liver, which is the main reason to know what it is.
descriptions.methaqualone: Quaaludes — a sedative widely prescribed for sleep in the 1960s and 70s, then banned almost everywhere after widespread misuse. It is essentially absent from the modern supply; pills sold under the name today are usually something else.
descriptions.lsa: The psychedelic compound in morning glory and Hawaiian baby woodrose seeds, which people eat for a long, dreamy, often nauseating experience. Seeds sold for planting are frequently coated with fungicides, and the nausea and vomiting are close to universal.
descriptions.grayanotoxin: A toxin in rhododendron and related plants, which turns up in honey made from their nectar. A small amount causes tingling and light-headedness. A little more drops heart rate and blood pressure hard enough to put people in hospital.
descriptions.salvinorin-a: The active compound in salvia divinorum, a sage plant, usually smoked as dried leaf. It produces an intense, disorienting experience that is over in minutes and that many people find frightening rather than pleasant. It is not related to any other psychedelic.
descriptions.ibogaine: A compound from the iboga shrub. It is used in Bwiti ceremonies in Gabon, and taken in unregulated clinics abroad to interrupt opioid dependence. It is not approved anywhere in the US. It disturbs heart rhythm, and accidents in clinic settings are documented. It is sold as a supervised medical treatment. It is not one.
descriptions.inhalants: A category rather than one drug: solvents, glues, aerosols, nitrous oxide, and the alkyl nitrites sold as poppers. What they share is being breathed in for a short high. What they do to the body differs completely between them, and some can stop the heart on a first use.
descriptions.phenobarbital: An old barbiturate, still prescribed for epilepsy and used in hospitals to manage severe alcohol withdrawal. It is a long-acting sedative. It works on the GABA-A receptor, holding the channel open itself. Benzodiazepines only boost the body's own signal, which is the difference between the two.
descriptions.pentobarbital: A barbiturate once prescribed for sleep, now used mainly in hospitals for anesthesia and seizures, and in veterinary euthanasia. Like all barbiturates it suppresses breathing and the safety margin is narrow.
descriptions.secobarbital: A barbiturate sleeping pill, widely prescribed decades ago and rare now. It suppresses breathing, and mixing it with alcohol is what made it notorious.
descriptions.flunitrazepam: Rohypnol — a strong benzodiazepine sleeping pill, prescribed in some countries and never approved in the US. It sedates heavily and interferes with memory formation. It is known mainly for drink spiking, and the manufacturer added a blue dye that colors a drink for that reason.
descriptions.midazolam: A short-acting benzodiazepine given in hospitals for sedation before procedures, and to stop prolonged seizures. It works fast and reliably erases memory of the procedure, which is intentional.
descriptions.temazepam: A benzodiazepine prescribed for sleep. Like all benzodiazepines it suppresses breathing alongside opioids and alcohol, and stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.bromazepam: A benzodiazepine prescribed for anxiety in many countries, though not in the US. It reduces anxiety and sedates, in the middle of its family for how long it lasts.
